#3133. Bono Bowl Review: U2 Delivers Halftime Goods & Hits On Netflix & NFL’s First Thanksgiving Eve Game, With A Little Help From Dolly Parton

Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics

No matter how many hits and tricks U2 pulled out of the hat at L.A.’s SoFi Stadium, today’s Bono Bowl on Netflix was always going to live in the shadow of the streamer’s square dancing filled Beyoncé Bowl from Christmas Day 2024.

Accepting the inevitable, the elder statesmen of anthem rock took their halftime spin on stage at the NFL’s first ever Thanksgiving Eve game to go full bread and circuses. Giving the people and the streamer what they wanted, the nine-minute show wasn’t as dramatic as the currently 13-13 match-up between the hometown L.A. Rams and the Green Bay Packers, but it didn’t have to be.

All U2 had to do tonight was show everyone they still have gas in the tank.

Under those criteria, in their first time headlining on Netflix, the Irish rockers succeeded.

Veering towards the tried and true, Bono, guitarist The Edge, bassiest Adam Clayton and drummer Larry Mullen Jr thundered through their Boomer classics of “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” The Joshua Tree’s “Where The Streets Have No Name” and MLK tribute “Pride (In The Name of Love).” Add to that a sprinkle of The Supremes “Stop! In the Name of Love” via some glorious vocals thrown in from teh Grammy nominated Womack Sisters and the beats of an on-field marching band and you have an All-American party — which is precisely what a NFL halftime show is supposed to be.

U2 performs 'Where The Streets Have No Name' at the NFL Thanksgiving Eve halftime show. pic.twitter.com/dXhj4KQbPk

In a nod to their latest release and the times we live in, the second song in the set poignantly was the “Torn” duet with Dolly Parton

Dolly Forever <3 U2 pays tribute to Dolly Parton with “Torn” during their halftime performance pic.twitter.com/c4CfeoQiXi

With the obvious exception of the inclusion of the late great Dolly, who was displayed on flowing curtains that came down from the stadium roof, it was a set that could have come almost anytime the last 40 years. In fact, besides “Torn” (Parton’s last recording), every song in U2’s Thanksgiving Eve set came from when Ronald Reagan was President.

Bono’s vow not to use backing tracks and the pre-halftime shot that Netflix showed of U2 heading through Sofi’s catacombs on gold carts sorta told you all you needed to know.

To their credit, unlike most Super Bowl halftime shows of the past dozen years, (and expected for Jay-Z’s Super Bowl LXI set on February 14 at Sofi), a relatively stripped down U2 didn’t bring on any super star guests for the L.A. crowd. Walking out on the field to a chorus, the usually-chatty band took the in-the-round stage with a “thank you for having us” and said little more.

Oddly ending a bit too quickly, tonight’s shindig came halfway through the NFL’s first Thanksgiving Eve match with the Rams battling it out with Packers at the L.A. team’s camera-ready stadium. A clear belt notch in the league’s desire to dramatically expand the incredibly lucrative football franchise, tonight’s much-hyped game between the Packers and the Rams was given all the gloss of a playoff clash or the Super Bowl itself by the Ted Sarandos and Greg Peter-run streamer.

Having already played a few warm-up gigs — like opening the November 14 Rock and Roll Hall of Fame ceremony — during the extensive promotional tour this month for their recently released Carnaval De Luz album, tonight gave U2 a further chance to reach fans old and new. Aided by a stage that was rolled out and set up in less than 8 minutes, a 52-foot telescopic camera crane and a specialty camera coming down from the Sofi roof, the Jesse Collins Entertainment-produced set had a very professional shine.

WHAT A PERFORMANCEU2 performs '(Pride) In The Name of Love' with The Womack Sisters at the NFL Thanksgiving Eve Halftime Show pic.twitter.com/ZBzEZ1SUIt

For a soaring-gesture band never shy of taking big stages in a big way, the global reach can only help U2 hawk a few more tickets for their upcoming Greatest Show on Earth tour. The tour begins in Mexico City in February. After shows in South America and Europe, the band and their unofficial 50th anniversary tour ends up in North America for a 15-stadium run starting in Miami on August 13.

At the same time, as the Rolling Stones, Bruce Springsteen and many other stadium-playing legacy acts will tell you, the role of old bands is to play the old hits — no matter how good or bad the latest album is. Bono, the Edge, Mullen and Clayton knew that back in 2002 when they played Super Bowl XXXVI in the aftermath of the 9/11 terror attacks. Using their Elevation Tour set at NOLA’s Superdome, U2 in less than 20-minutes whipped off “Beautiful Day,” “MLK” and “Where The Streets Have No Name” and paid tribute via curtain with the names of the fallen on it to those who lost their lives that horrible day in NYC.

One of the biggest bands in the world for 40 years, U2 haven’t toured since 2019, and they had a bit to prove tonight, as they made clear.

Yet, the GameDay halftime show wasn’t their first time on stage this decade.

A 40-show stint at Vegas’ Sphere starting in September 2023 saw the band pulling it off Zoo TV style, even with an injured Mullen sitting it out. Still, a big live draw since the mid-1980s no matter how their records charted, the Irving and Jeffrey Azoff-managed U2 are leaving no opportunity unexplored this year in a hope to return to relevance.

Even Sofi itself got in on the act on Wednesday.

We are excited to welcome @U2 for their premiere appearance at SoFi Stadium during today's halftime show 🏈 And even more excited for their return on October 1 & 2! Tickets on sale on December 4 on Ticketmaster 🎟️ pic.twitter.com/KnB9CkgIQp

With ads galore and L.A. beauty shots tonight, Netflix has finally worked out most of the kinks that marred some of their past live sports events. Fueled by play-by-play from Noah Eagle and analysis from Hall-of-Famer Luke Kuechly, the primetime result so far delivered a slick and seamless product that moved at the pace of the action on the field. Simply put (and hear me Jeff Bezos), Netflix equaled what ESPN and Monday Night Football have been doing for ages — which is no small feat when you consider that the streamer’s initial live sporting event was just over three years ago with the mash-up golf tournament The Netflix Cup.

From the big picture perspective, tonight’s game and that halftime show can’t but help Netflix’s ongoing bid to FIFA for the 2030 World Cup. For U2, the ride may be vintage, but turns out there’s still quite a bit of gas in the old tank.

#3132. The Best Black Friday Deals on Smartwatches and Fitness Trackers

Black Friday sales are now in full swing. I've been keeping an eye on all the best fitness trackers and smartwatch deals so that you can snag the best possible price from now until the end of Cyber Monday (Nov. 30). Whether you want a full-featured fitness smartwatch or a more recovery-focused tracker, here are the discounts you can find right now, including on brands like Apple, Oura, Garmin, and more.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is a worthy competitor to the Oura Ring 5, with an included high-capacity charging case and no subscription. You can read Beth's comparison of the two here: most people would probably prefer the Oura, but the pros and cons are nuanced and you, dear reader, may be exactly the person the Ultrahuman is best for. The silver color is only $299 in this Black Friday deal, with other colors going for $379. The ring normally retails for $479, so that's $100 to $180 off, depending on color. That price includes a charging case and all the basic functionality of the ring; some extras require a subscription.

This is a rare deal from Pebble! An email from the company states "We don’t do sales. Black Friday is the one exception each year." The Pebble Time 2 is on sale for $200, down from $225 regular price. This is the brand's rectangular watch, with a heart rate sensor, and an always-on MIP (e-paper) screen. The Pebble 2 Duo (a "do-over" version of the Pebble of yore) is also on sale, for $124, down from $149.

The Oura Ring 5 is at its lowest ever price: $299 for black and silver, $399 for all other colors. These are the lowest prices ever for these rings, which usually go for $399 and $499, respectively. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I've tried, although it's worth noting it requires a $5.99/month subscription fee.

For an even cheaper deal, the older Oura Ring 4 is $249—a full $100 off its list price of $349. If you opt for "stealth" (matte black), the price is $279; for gold, it's $286.61, down from $399. While this model has since been replaced by the Oura Ring 5, it's still an accurate and comfortable smart ring—especially if tracking your sleep is your priority.

Whoop may be one of the most expensive smart bands out there, thanks to its subscription-only model. But that price is particularly low right now, since the Peak membership that normally goes for $239 is now $199. Peak is the middle tier, and it's the one Beth recommends. While you can get Whoop One for $189 in this sale, the $10 you save isn't really worth it given the features you'd be missing. We also wouldn't normally recommend Whoop Life, since its ECG readings and blood pressure estimates aren't really worth the extra cost. That said, if you do want it, the Life tier is $299 right now instead of $359.

The new Luna band is on sale for $119.20, down from a normal price of $149. The Luna band is made by Indian smartwatch company Noise, the same company behind the Luna Ring that Beth reviewed last year. The ring is no longer available in the U.S., but the band is. It's a Whoop-style screenless fitness tracker, potentially a worthy competitor to the Fitbit Air and other smart bands.

This is the brand-new Apple Watch model, and it's actually worth the upgrade. One of the biggest reasons is that the Series 12's new processor (called, confusingly, the S11 chip) supports some features older Apple Watches can't, and a good rule of thumb is that whenever there's a break in software compatibility, it makes sense to get the newer model. Right now, we're seeing it for as low as $299, down from the list price of $399. (And if you're stuck deciding between an Apple Watch and a Fitbit, Beth breaks it all down in her comparison of the two watches.)

The Google Pixel Watch 5 has been marked down by $100, starting at $299.99 for the version that normally retails for $399.99. Each model is $100 off its regular price, including the LTE and Wifi-only models of both sizes.

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is Nothing's latest smartwatch, and it incorporates AI features powered by ChatGPT; you can currently pick it up at a major discount. Originally $99, you can get the CMF Watch 3 Pro for $55. This is the lowest price this smartwatch has been.

If you're looking specifically for a sporty, outdoors watch, Garmin sets the standard. (You could definitely call Meredith something of a Garmin enthusiast.) Here are the best Black Friday deals on Garmin watches that we've seen so far:

The 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 is 249.99 (down from $449.99). The 1.2-inch color AMOLED display makes the screen more readable in bright daylight conditions, and battery life is best-in-class—a must for those going off-grid.

The Garmin Fēnix 8 in titanium with a gray band is $749.99 (down from $999.99). While this is last year's model, it's a perfectly solid option if you don't specifically need the titanium case or the latest mapping engine in the latest Fenix 9 Pro.

The Garmin Forerunner 265 is $299.99 (down from $449.99). Although it isn't the latest and greatest anymore, this is still a fan favorite among Garmin users. It's a step above entry-level options, with dual-band GPS, power meter compatibility, and advanced analytics (like training status).

Meredith's beloved Forerunner 970, the top-of-the-line Garmin for serious runners, is $649.99 right now, down from an original price of $749.99.

Yes, Garmin is one of the best brands when it comes to rugged sports watches and fitness trackers. The Forerunner line, especially, is a go-to pick for accurate and reliable GPS tracking for runners.

My pick would be the Garmin Forerunner 265 for $299.99. It's a slightly older model, but still works well and is packed with features for runners.

There are! Check out the Apple Watch deals above. If you can't decide, my pick would be the brand-new Series 12 at $299. This one has step counting and will soon be getting the slightly creepy Siri Recaps (which you can disable if you'd rather not deal with them).

#3130. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “The Long-Distance Surgeon.”

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

#3129. I’m hunting the best PS5 deals LIVE — latest discounts on games and accessories from Walmart, Best Buy, Gamestop and more

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Staff picked deals:1. Quick Links2. Editor's Choice3. Latest updates

Finding a PS5 console isn't easy right now, but the same isn't true for Black Friday sales on games and peripherals! So if you want to build out your PS5 library or need a new controller or headset to enjoy your system more, now is the best time to shop.

Right now, you can get a PS5 DualSense controller for $20 off, while the Razer Raiju V3 Pro controller is $63 off. Game-wise, PS5 exclusives like Marvel's Wolverine are $20 off. Third-party games like the excellent 007 First Light are now 50% off via the PlayStation Store.

Black Friday deals will likely go into overdrive during Black Friday proper, but even today, you can save big. To that end, I and the other gamers on Tom's Guide are on the lookout for everything that appears and will update this live blog with the latest and greatest PS5 deals.

Anyone who loved Returnal will appreciate this cinematic follow-up. Saros is a relentless rogue-lite shooter blending spectacle with tight, bullet-hell combat. It improves on some of the rough edges of its predecessor and, while it pulls a couple of punches, you'll be saying “one more run” more often than not.

Stellar Blade is a hack-and-slash action-adventure game in the best spirit of the genre. It takes full advantage of the PS5's horsepower and serves up thrilling combat sequences and an engaging story. The graphics aren't half bad-looking, either.

Marvel’s Wolverine is a slickly presented superhero adventure that casts players as the most famous of the X-Men. Combat is extremely violent (as the character demands) but we did find it quite repetitive. At least the enjoyable (if predictable) original comic book story gives players a reason to keep going.

Sony’s standard PS5 pad remains one of the best controllers around thanks to its responsive haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. Standard colourways, including white, midnight black, cosmic red, and galactic purple, are down to $54 here, beating PlayStation Direct’s sale price.

Sony's first set of PlayStation wireless earbuds, the Pulse Explore, are discounted this Black Friday. These are a great pick if you don't want to wear a bulky over-ear headset while playing multiplayer games.

The PS5 is hard to come by this Black Friday, and if you do find one, it's at retail. That stings, but it doesn't hurt to get a PS5 when you can. This model is the base PS5 Slim, now the cheapest PS5 available. It comes with an 825GB SSD.

Welcome to our PS5 deals live blog — and we're getting started with one of the best PS5 games you can play on your console today at a staggering 50% off.

Our review called 007 First Light, “the finest James Bond video game in nearly 30 years,” and right now it's half price at the PlayStation Store ahead of Black Friday. If you haven't played it yet, it's a new take on Fleming's iconic spy, putting players in the role of a young, up-and-coming agent making his way through nail-biting missions, thrilling plot twists, and cinematic moments. I wonder if Robert Pattinson is a fan?

For those that want their gaming experience with a side order of whimsy, I give you: Astro Bot. This charming platformer is a fan favorite with PS5 gamers and if you haven't gotten around to playing it yet, now you can do so for a lot less.

Walmart currently has the game on sale for $39 — saving you just over $19. The adventure takes you through some classic PlayStation-themed levels and, while it's short, it's a really enjoyable game that makes full use of the DualSense controller's haptic feedback.

Sony's first set of PlayStation wireless earbuds, the Pulse Explore, are already discounted for Black Friday. You can grab them for $119 at Best Buy right now.

These are a great pick if you don't want to wear bulky over-ear headsets while gaming, and they can also double as standard Bluetooth earbuds for your phone while you're out. The only downside is that with up to 5 hours of battery life on a single charge, you may be reaching for the charging case (with an additional 10 hours) sooner than you'd like.

Well, it's obviously no surprise that GTA 6 hasn't been discounted anywhere. I guess the eight or nine PlayStation gamers that haven't bought Rockstar's mega-hit yet are probably pretty bummed.

I'll keep an eye out for any GTA-related discounts but, in the meantime, have you read our review? You can check it out here. Spoiler alert, it scored pretty high.

Do you remember the first couple of PlayStation consoles? If you wanted to have a buddy game with you, you needed to spring for a "Multitap" — Google it if I've lost you. Regardless, my point is that you need more than one controller in your life.

And if you're going to get another pad, it makes sense to get the best. The DualSense Edge is Sony's first official "pro" controller and the premium version of the DualSense. It's expensive, but that's where this Amazon deal comes in — bringing it down by 15%. You can fully customize your play experience by tweaking stick sensitivity and dead zones, and even remap each button individually. Plus, it includes adjustable back buttons. Nice!

Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced is a game I'm really tempted by. I missed it the first time around, and I love a good pirate adventure. Right now, Amazon has knocked this game down to just $30 for Black Friday.

In our full review of the game, we said Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced offers (almost) everything you could want from a remake: "It looks stunning, adds worthwhile new content, makes loads of smart improvements, and the simple joys of being a ruthless pirate on the open seas haven’t faded with time."

If you need a proper simulation racing game, you can't do better on PS5 than Gran Turismo 7. This game offers polished racing, a ridiculous number of cars, plenty of customization options, ultra-realistic graphics, a wide variety of soundtracks, and impeccable style. At this reduced price, it's totally worth checking out.

Marvel's Wolverine is the big PS5 exclusive of the year, but it certainly received mixed reception. So if you were on the fence, you might want to check it out now that Amazon is selling it for $20 off. I enjoyed my time with the game, but I do agree with some of the criticism. That said, I think paying $49 for what you get here is worth it.

Saros is the other major PS5 exclusive of 2026, and it somewhat fell off the radar after launch. If you're curious about Housemarque's latest bullet-hell roguelike, you can grab Saros for just $39. This is easily one of the toughest games out there, so prepare to die a lot until you get used to the gameplay loop.

Pragmata is one of my favorite games of the year. It was easy to recommend at its original $59 price, but it's a no-brainer at $39. The puzzle-based combat mechanic, which forces you to engage enemies strategically, is engrossing once you get used to it, and the story is heartwarming. Do yourself a favor and don't miss out on Pragmata.

If you need an extra controller, you can get the DualSense for $54 right now. Various colors are on sale, so take a look and see which one you like best.

Silent Hill: Townfall is the best the survival horror series has been in 25 years. Developer Screen Burn takes the series into first-person with a new remote Scottish town setting, breathing fresh energy into the franchise. But while some things change, Silent Hill’s phenomenal atmosphere, visuals, and sound design remain. It’s a horrific, often unsettling experience, but it’s one that I never wanted to stop playing.

While Street Fighter 6 is already pretty affordable at $19, you can save an additional $5 with this Black Friday deal. While a slew of new fighting games are out there, SF6 remains the king thanks to its robust combat mechanics and expansive single-player mode. Capcom keeps adding updates, so this game has staying power.

Lego Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight takes everything folks know about Batman from popular culture and filters it through the tried-and-true Lego formula. Whether you're a fan of Batman or Lego games, there's a lot to love in this charming adventure.

The SteelSeries Arctis Nova 7 Gen 2 brings some important upgrades over the original model, including a 40% boost to battery life and simultaneous wireless connectivity. Sound quality is decent, especially for competitive gaming, where the headset’s bright treble shines. The companion software is slick and useful, and the headset is comfortable to wear. The mic is fine for gaming but a little tinny (so streamers beware). Still, a solid headset and a welcome upgrade over the original.

Star Wars Outlaws delivers a true Star Wars experience, with four worlds featuring expansive maps and side quests for hours of fun. Space combat and general gunplay are solid, though rare stealth moments can be frustrating. Several technical issues and crashes can also hurt immersion.

I'll never miss a chance to recommend Elden Ring during Black Friday, especially at this discounted price! Right now, you can get FromSoftware's open-world epic for just $19. The core game features expansive maps filled with secrets, memorable boss battles, and an engaging multiplayer system that lets you tackle the game's horrors with friends. Don't miss this sale if you haven't played one of the finest games of this generation.

You can't play Mario Kart on PS5, but you can get the next best thing with Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds! As we said in our Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds review, this game is packed with chaos and fun, with smooth drifting and air tricks. CrossWorlds makes a big splash as a multi-platform karting game.

The Razer Raiju V3 Pro is a mighty controller for PS5 and PC. The TMR sticks provide precise movement control while eliminating the risk of stick drift. It's highly customizable and very comfortable for long gaming sessions. Although it’s missing some proprietary PS5 features, it’s the gamepad to beat for esports and a worthy rival to Sony's own DualSense Edge.

Metaphor: ReFantazio feels like a breath of fresh air. Yes, it borrows systems from both Persona and Shin Megami Tensei, but it also offers plenty of new ideas in Atlus’ fantasy-inspired world. While it runs on an older engine, its stylized visuals are impressive. It’s not the most graphically demanding game, but the attention to detail and strong art design make up for that.

Marvel's Spider-Man 2 on PS5 sees Peter Parker and Miles Morales web-swing into action for another stellar superhero romp across Marvel's New York. Swap between the Spider-Men and deploy their new powers as you take on new villains from Spidey's rogues' gallery in this excellent action game that looks truly stunning on PS5 and especially on PS5 Pro.

Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 finally brings the classic Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots from the PS3 and to modern consoles. In addition, the collection includes Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker and Metal Gear Solid: Ghost Babel.

The HyperX Cloud III S Wireless is a comfortable headset that makes games feel immersive with fantastic sound quality thanks to its 53mm drivers. It includes a detachable boom mic and a built-in backup mic, and its battery life is among the best we’ve seen. However, customization options are limited; there’s no Xbox variant, and the earcups can get hot.

Final Fantasy Tactics: The Ivalice Chronicles is a triumphant remake/remaster. Featuring enhanced HD graphics, a fully voiced script, and numerous quality-of-life improvements, it's the definitive way to play this beloved tactical JRPG classic. It releases on PS5, Nintendo Switch, and Xbox Series X/S on September 30. You can pre-order it now.

Ghost of Yotei is another high-quality and seriously cinematic PS5 exclusive. It offers few new ideas compared to its predecessor, and the segmented main campaign makes the story feel repetitive. However, what it lacks in originality it makes up for with brilliantly brutal combat, a sizeable open world stuffed with distractions and stunning visuals, especially on PS5 Pro.

If the full-price release of The Last of Us Part 1 put you off retracing Ellie and Joel's steps in this gorgeous remake of one of PlayStation's best-known titles, now's your chance to pick it up for a huge $41 off. The remake features improved visuals, new animation, and more tactical, more aggressive enemies, making exploration of the post-apocalyptic USA even more stressful and engaging.

The Sony Inzone M9 II is an excellent 27-inch 4K monitor for console and PC gaming. With its sleeker design and higher 160Hz refresh rate, it’s a clear improvement over its predecessor. Right now, Sony is selling this monitor for $250 off during Black Friday! I gave it 4.5 out of 5 stars in my Sony Inzone M9 II review, so I highly recommend it!

PlayStation's excellent PS Pulse headsets cost $99 but the high-end, even better Pulse Elite are on sale right now for just $109, down from $149.

In our PS Pulse Elite review, we praise the big sound from the Tempest Audio 3D and a comfortable fit.

There's been recent derision over the "dad game" because of the absolute glut of games where the main character has to learn or relearn how to be a father. Think God of War or The Last of Us as two heavy hitters in the genre.

Fortunately, most are pretty good, and Capcom's Pragmata, the latest entry in the trope, is excellent and worth your time. Plus, it's on sale for $40.

Don't believe me? Then read our Pragmata review, where we called it the surprise hit for 2026.

I've been a Dual-whatever apologist for years, but I don't really have to defend the DualSense Edge. It's Sony's high-end PS5 controller that is customizable from the triggers to the sticks and even the faceplate. Plus it comes with a nice carrying case.

Normally, the price is the biggest drawback at $200, but for Black Friday, Sony is knocking $30 off. Not quite the $50 I'd like but better than two hundo.

I like to thrift from time to time, but I'm very specific about what I'll actually purchase, and electronics are one area where I really need to check the device.

However, many companies offer certified refurbishment programs including Sony. You can get up to $100 off refurbished PS5 consoles directly from PlayStation.

Currently, you can get the PS5 Slim, PS5 digital edition, and the original PS5 disc edition for $100 off the original price.

Alternatively, Best Buy also sells refurbished PS5s through the Geek Squad. Though Best Buy discounts are far less.

It is absurd how much fun Star Wars: Galactic Racer is, from playing to watching. I can't remember the last game that was worth buying just to watch other people play. I literally stop and watch whenever it pops up in my social media feeds.

Trust me, it's worthy of the podium; forget GTA 6, you need to go to space.

If you haven't, pick this one up for your collection.

If you're a sports gamer but held off on upgrading to this year's editions, now may be the time to splurge.

Just about every EA Sports title is on sale, as well as the latest 2K NBA game and, for those missing baseball, MLB The Show.

In fact, the only sports game of the US Big Four that isn't on sale is NHL 26, still at the full $69 price. Sorry, puck fans. But we can swap in the world's game with FC 26 which is discounted.

Before GTA 6 launched last week, it was nearly impossible to find a PS5 console. At one point, used PS5 Pros were selling for $1500 on GameStop and Walmart third-party markets.

However, this week there appears to be an eensy bit more stock. The PS5 Pro is still unbelievably unavailable.

As of this posting, I'm seeing two options available on Walmart and Best Buy (maybe).

The Best Buy options are confusing because it shows as available but there's also a queue. You're rolling the dice here. Both also feature 3rd party sellers, so be wary.

I played the original Kingdom Hearts on the family PS2 way back in 2002 with my brother. Weirdly, the strongest memory I have is the silly volleyball game at the starting island when you're still on the beach. Perhaps too much FFX bled into that time.

Anyway, I'm seriously considering the Kingdom Hearts collection I-III, especially since I'm not sure where that original PS2 is, possibly with my brother.

#3128. Apple Home accessories: Here are my five top picks for your smart home

Apple Home is kicking off a new era with Siri AI-driven products like HomeView, making it a great time to upgrade your smart home with Apple Home-compatible accessories. Here are my top five picks.

iOS 27 upgraded Apple’s HomeKit Secure Video service (included with iCloud+) in several key ways. You’ll now get searchable videos, highlighted clips, 4K support, and more.

I have two recommendations for HomeKit Secure Video-compatible cameras. The main difference is video quality, and whether they’re designed for outdoor use or only indoors.

Smart locks have always offered convenience, but with the advent of Ultra Wideband-supported locks, they’re better than ever.

Aqara’s U400 smart lock was among the first to introduce Ultra Wideband, which enables your door to lock and unlock automatically when it senses your presence. Unlike prior smart lock automations that relied on Bluetooth, Ultra Wideband offers excellent reliability and precision for a great overall experience.

Want to open your garage door with a quick Siri command, or via CarPlay or the Home app on iPhone? Smart garage door openers with Apple Home support can deliver that, and my recommendation is the meross MSG150HK.

meross says the MSG150HK is compatible with “the vast majority of Chamberlain, Lift-Master, and Craftsman brand openers.” And it supports security features like automatic notifications when your door is left open, or every time it opens and closes.

Smart plugs are often a gateway to building out a smart home. And my favorite option, both for cost and convenience, is Tapo’s multipack of smart plugs.

Tapo sells its smart plug in a 2-pack at a great price—currently only $8 per plug. These plugs are compact and offer seamless, quick setup through the Home app without needing a separate app.

Controlling your thermostat entirely from your iPhone or a HomeView can prove extremely convenient. That convenience can also save you money by making it easier to stay on top of your electricity usage.

Aqara’s W200 smart thermostat is a beautifully designed, easy-to-use accessory that comes with a bonus Apple feature that’s hard to find: Adaptive Temperature, which can remove lots of the need to manually update the thermostat.

What are your top Apple Home accessory recommendations? Let us know in the comments.

#3127. ‘South Park’ Celebrates ‘GTA VI’ But Outages, AI Data Centers & Zombie Kenny Stand In The Way In Season 29 Finale

As the long wait for Grand Theft Auto VI finally ends, South Park‘s celebration was cut short on this week’s episode.

In the finale “City Endings,” outages hit the town (currently rebranded as South America for Season 29) thanks to the AI data centers of Billionaire Weenietown that moved into Butters’ backyard after Mayor McDaniels cut a deal to bring them to town.

A mob visits the mayor, who instead of taking responsibility, leads them to believe the outages are “definitely cyber attacks by the Chinese.” That prompts the mob to stake out Mr. Kim’s City Parlor, where they each end up getting a massage with a “city ending.” Watch on Deadline

Meanwhile, Kyle, Stan and Cartman are visited by the ghost of Kenny, who previously died when a bomb strapped to his e-bike exploded.

The trio gives Butters a visit after remembering his connectivity issues while trying to watch Dr. Pimple Popper videos. It turns out, Butters is no longer affected by the outages as he’s since been getting some kickbacks from Billionaire Weenietown, including a massive GTA VI setup.

In the middle of Butters’ gameplay, zombie Kenny appears on the screen, breaking out like Samara in The Ring to deliver a message to his friends.

The episode culminates with the kids confronting the cops and the mayor, only to find out they were all complicit in Kenny’s death when they allowed the billionaires to come to South Park.

Ultimately, Mayor McDaniels takes responsibility for the billionaires ruining the town but sends Mr. Kim to space on WeenieX in order to appease the town. The show ends with “America” falling off the South Park sign after they rolled over to change the town’s name for Trump.

South Park‘s finale wrapped up its Billionaire Weenietown storyline with some more topical jabs, following the massively unprecedented release of GTA VI, as well as the ongoing nationwide outages, which the government has chalked up to many networks changing over to AI systems.

#3126. These Are the Best Black Friday 2026 Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

Score the year's biggest savings during the Black Friday sale on the best e-reader deals as they launch in real time. Follow our Black Friday Live Blog for live coverage of the absolute best deals, flash sales, and tech savings. For a deep dive into top-rated offers, expert buying guides, and exclusive discounts, explore our Best Black Friday Amazon Tech Deals page.

Amazon's Black Friday sale is in full swing, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

If you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.)

If you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

For about $30 more than the X4 Classic, you can upgrade to the Xteink X4 Pro, which happens to be Lifehacker's e-reader Gift of the Year pick. It offers all the perks of the other Xteink devices, with two critical quality-of-life upgrades: A touchscreen for easier navigation, and a temperature-adjustable front light so you can read it in a dark room. (Less obviously, it also has a slightly faster processor that makes the whole thing feel a little snappier.) Right now, the X4 Pro is at its lowest price ever when ordered directly from Xteink: $84, or around 15% off the usual $99 price.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

#3125. Skip the knockoffs: Real PITAKA aramid fiber cases start at $18.99 this Black Friday

Scroll through Amazon for five minutes and you’ll find dozens of $10–20 cases that look, through a thumbnail, almost identical to $50+ aramid fiber ones. Same dark weave, same slim profile, same pitch.

Once you actually snap one onto a phone, the differences are obvious. You handle your phone for hours every day, so rough seams around the charging port, awkward cutouts, low-quality materials will make you regret your purchase instantly. With PITAKA’s Black Friday sale taking up to 30% off selected cases, it’s worth breaking down what actually separates a real aramid case from a cheap lookalike, why you should spent the extra money on PITAKA’s high-quality cases.

Plenty of budget cases get the woven look by printing a pattern onto plain plastic. If you’re looking for that style, go for it, but it won’t behave like woven aramid fiber, which lets a case stay rigid and thin without adding much weight.

Even genuine aramid cases aren’t all made the same way. The weave, resin, thickness, and surface finish all change how a case feels in use. PITAKA uses woven aramid fiber in two main weights: 600D and 1500D. Those numbers measure yarn density; the finer 600D weave feels a bit smoother and produces a slightly thinner shell than 1500D. Whatever case you choose, look past the word “premium” and check whether the maker actually spells out what the case is made of.

Most aramid cases stick to plain black and gray. PITAKA’s Fusion Weaving method blends colored fibers and multiple weave styles directly into the shell instead of printing a graphic on the outside. PITAKA says the process requires tight control over fabric tension and how fibers cross between layers. In practice, it means you can pick something colorful like the Sunset colorway without giving up the feel of woven fiber, or stick with classic Black & Grey if you prefer a quieter look.

Online listings spend almost all their time showing off the back of a case, even though your fingers spend just as much time on the sides, buttons, and bottom edge. An awkward camera cutout makes quick shots annoying, a tight port opening fights bulkier charging cables, and sharp edges dig into your hand on a long call.

Rather than selling one shell in ten colors, PITAKA splits its lineup into three builds:

If you use a magnetic charger, wallet, or grip, how the magnets are built into the case matters just as much as the outer material. Sticking a separate magnet ring inside a shell usually adds extra layers and thickness.

PITAKA’s Amber Magnet Film process bonds coated magnets directly with the aramid fiber and resin under heat and pressure. That keeps the magnets enclosed without bulking up the case, which is the kind of detail you won’t spot in a photo but will notice in your pocket.

Spending more on a case doesn’t guarantee it’s better, and plenty of $20 cases are completely fine. Genuine aramid fiber by itself doesn’t guarantee better drop protection either. A thin shell like Edge is made for people who hate bulky cases. If drop protection is your main concern, look at a cushioned option like Cairn or Summa, and compare actual edge coverage and model-specific testing instead of judging by price or material alone.

What you’re really paying for with a higher-end aramid case is how it feels and fits every time you pick up your phone.

If you already want a thinner, better-finished case, Black Friday takes some of the sting out of the price. PITAKA’s Amazon offers run November 19–30, with discounts varying by device and colorway:

Buying directly from the PITAKA official website? Code PTKPR12 takes an extra 5% off from November 10 through December 31. It’s separate from the Amazon sale, so double-check eligible products and your final total at checkout.

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

The BenQ ScreenBar Max lights my whole desk - a game changer on many levels

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As with many home workers, I’m very lucky to have a dedicated office space that doubles as a PC gaming space when the working day is done, but as the nights draw closer and it gets much darker sooner (at least here in the UK), I’ve been looking for alternative options to keeping my room lighting on to avoid overpowering my eyes.

Enter BenQ, with the manufacturer offering its ScreenBar® Max to check out. With it, I’ve gone from being desperate to get out of the office before it gets dark to never wanting to leave.

I’ve used multiple screen-mounted lighting options in the past, but it would be fair to say the ScreenBar Max goes further than many of its contemporaries.

I work nine-hour days and often hop back on in the evenings to get additional projects finished, and that means I’ve been looking for something to help me do my best work regardless of time of day.

The trouble is that many of these light bars illuminate one spot on a desk, focusing on a relatively small section of the workspace. That’s particularly troublesome in my use case because I have a dual-monitor setup, meaning there’s more surface area to cover, and they’ve just not been up to the task - until now.

BenQ’s ScreenBar Max is wide enough to allow for minimal glare since it’s not centred on a specific spot, and has done a great job of keeping me focused and locked in well into the evenings.

This is achieved with what BenQ calls its ASYM-TriZone Light and a 36-degree shielding angle, which prevents the light from pointing directly at the user. This means the light stays where you want it to be (across your desk) and not in your peepers.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With up to 700 lux of brightness and a colour temperature that moves from 2700K to 6000K, it’ll automatically adjust to find the ANSI-recommended 1:3 contrast ratio.

I’m also pleased to say that backlighting on offer is very welcome. Too often, working on a desk with a light bar can feel a little like working in a cave, and this helps illuminate the space behind your desk. It’s a small touch, but it’s very welcome.

My favourite feature of the BenQ ScreenBar Max might be that it slides out handily from the stand to cover more of the desk.

This means if you have a compatible webcam that allows for desk view, and you’re demonstrating something on your desktop, you can ensure it’s well-illuminated. As someone who plays trading card games with friends online, it’s nice to be able to ensure my playspace is the most reliably lit of anyone in the match.

The ScreenBar Max can achieve this because, rather than putting extra weight on the top of your desk, it sits behind—either on a desk clamp or a dedicated stand—meaning it’s not tied to your monitor setup in the way traditional light bars can be.

And, while other options have you fussing with buttons and dials to get them activated, the BenQ ScreenBar Max uses the same sensors that BenQ tells me are found in autonomous systems. This means I can walk into the office with my morning coffee, and “voila!” - the lighting activates, automatically adjusted to my space.

As I mentioned earlier, the ScreenBar Max has me dreading those cold winter months less than I was, and I’m almost excited to do my work in a space so well lit for the first time in a long time.

The BenQ ScreenBar Max is available now for £239 from BenQ online and selected retailers.

#3120. Lauren Ash & Mae Martin Among Cast Of Shozer’s Adult Animation High-School Comedy ‘Dirts’

EXCLUSIVE: Lauren Ash (Superstore) and Mae Martin (Wayward) have been cast in Dirts, an ensemble adult animated high-school comedy series for New Metric Media‘s streaming service Shozer.

They will appear alongside the likes of Ash’s Superstore co-star Mark McKinney, Mark Little (Gary and His Demons) and Ryan Belleville (Workin’ Moms).

The show, set to premiere in winter 2027, follows Gus (Little) and Brus (Belleville), two deeply unpopular vegetable teenagers trying to survive life at Leguma Beach High, where high-society vine vegetables mingle with scrappy root transplants. The unlikely friends have to navigate the indignities of adolescence in a world where school politics can get particularly rotten. Related Stories Casting Lauren Ash, Mae Martin & Randall Park Join Crave Comedy 'Meatballs' News Samantha Bee Sitcom 'The Ambassador' Toplines CBC's Latest Slate

Ash plays Sproutabella, Martin is Trevin Stems and McKinney Principal Corny. Also in the voice cast are Kyle Dooley (Cupcake & Dino: General Services) as Eggmilio and Butternut; Evany Rosen (Total Dramarama) as Cheryl and Snap Pea; Kayla Lorette (Doomlands) as Pep and Ms. Jicama; Rodrigo Fernandez-Stoll (BlackBerry) as Janitor McKale and Theatre Squash; and Chelsea Clark (Ginny & Georgia) as Gabe.

Dane Clark, Viveno Caldinelli and Mark Montefiore co-created the show, with Caldinelli directing. New Metric Media is the producer in partnership with Little Black Stone Studios. Ariel Yang and Max Wolfond are the producers for New Metric, with Tysen Potter in the same role for Little Black Stone. Production will cater for vertical and horizontal viewing, and you can watch a first-look clip above.

Dirts toplines the latest slate for Shozer, the YouTube comedy channel brand that Shoresy and Letterkenny producer New Metric launched last year.

Also greenlit is The Historical History of Canada, a mockumentary series that takes a twisted and satirical look at the most infamous moments in Canadian history. These will include the mysterious fire that destroyed the Parliament building in 1916 and the Toronto Maple Leafs’ latest Stanley Cup win. New Metric’s Lana Maclin, Alona Metzer and Liv Berkowitz are producing.

Elevator Comedy is a 30-part series of 45-second episodes that will give emerging comedy talent a platform, with performers put in close quarters with the audience. As with Dirts, it’s being produced for vertical and horizontal viewing.

The Eh-List, New Metric’s stand-up comedy strand, is also getting specials from Just For Laughs regular Daniel Tirado, veteran comic Alex Wood and viral sensation Drew Behm.

Shozer debuted last year with a slate of shows and films including Lionsgate’s Running Wilde, Van Wilder: Party Liaison and Zack and Miri Make A Porno, along with Letterkenny‘s first YouTube outing, LetterkennyProblems.

“We’ve spent years building comedy franchises and seeing what happens when audiences connect with great characters and creators,” said Montefiore, CEO of New Metric. “With Shozer, we’re applying that experience to a D2C model where we can discover new talent, invest in original ideas and build audience communities.

“We want Shozer to become a trusted destination for comedy, where people come to discover their next favourite creator or series. And by developing and owning that IP from the outset, we have the flexibility to grow those properties across multiple platforms, formats and consumer experiences.”

#3118. AirTag 2 has two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade

AirTag 2 (now only $18, down from $29) launched earlier this year after a five-year wait, and in my experience there are two big improvements that make it worth the upgrade.

Precision Finding is Apple’s best AirTag feature, letting you get step-by-step, highly precise directions to your lost item. But with the original AirTag, you had to be in fairly close proximity before you could benefit from Precision Finding.

With AirTag 2, Apple added a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip that makes Precision Finding now available from up to 1.5x farther away than before. It’s a huge increase that I’ve definitely noticed.

This expansion of Precision Finding to greater distances means the feature is now available a lot more often than with the old AirTag. For this reason alone, I highly recommend AirTag 2.

When you’re trying to find a lost item, Precision Finding isn’t the only tool AirTag offers. There’s also a built-in speaker that can play a sound, triggered by your iPhone, to help you track it down.

With AirTag 2, Apple has made the built-in speaker 50% louder than before. The company says this enables hearing it from up to twice as far away.

I’ve been impressed by how loud the AirTag speaker is able to get now. Between the new speaker and upgraded Precision Finding, Apple has made AirTag 2 better in the ways that users are likely to care about most.

You can buy AirTag 2 for $18 on Amazon (regularly $29) for a limited time.

Have you upgraded to AirTag 2? What’s your experience been like? Let us know in the comments.

#3114. Ariane 6 launches 36 Amazon Leo satellites nine days after Vulcan failure

Amazon Leo now has 432 satellites in orbit, Ars Technica reports. Europe is weighing how to build more Ariane 6 rockets, with a decision possible next month.

An Ariane 6 upper stage being lifted onto DLR’s P5.2 test stand, February 2021

Amazon is moving its next SpaceX launch for Amazon Leo forward to December. On Tuesday, Europe’s Ariane 6 put 36 more of its satellites into orbit. An Amazon official told Stephen Clark of Ars Technica that the Falcon 9 flight was originally due next year. Several more Falcon 9 launches will follow in quick succession.

SpaceX also runs Starlink, the network Amazon Leo is built to compete with. Starlink has more than 11,000 satellites, according to Ars.

The Ariane 6 lifted off from French Guiana at about 6:15am New York time, Summer Maxwell reported for Bloomberg. It released all 36 satellites about two hours later. It was the rocket’s 10th flight and Arianespace’s fourth for Amazon. Arianespace has now launched 136 Amazon satellites.

The launch came nine days after a Vulcan rocket failure destroyed 40 Amazon Leo satellites. United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan is Amazon’s main launch provider. It cannot fly until an investigation led by the US Federal Aviation Administration ends. Blue Origin’s New Glenn has not flown since May, and its return to flight has slipped to early next year.

Amazon Leo now has 432 satellites in orbit, Ars reported. Amazon has booked 108 launches to deploy 3,232 satellites, and 17 have flown so far, with one failure. Amazon has not yet started its internet service, Bloomberg reported. In 2025 it had said the service would start that year.

Amazon added six Ariane 6 launches in September, taking its total with Arianespace to 24. Arianespace plans to raise the rocket’s cadence to 12 launches a year by about 2030, according to Bloomberg.

Europe’s factories can support up to nine or ten Ariane 6 flights a year, Ars reported. Arianespace is likely to reach six this year, with one more before the end of December. European ministers are weighing plans to build more Ariane 6 rockets, and a decision could come next month.

Amazon built its 1,000th satellite in October. Hundreds now wait in storage for a ride to orbit, according to Ars.

Black Friday deals start showing up long before Black Friday actually arrives, and it's easy to shop most sales online without ever having to set foot in a store.
